item.title: Clancy’s Defense Lawyer Asks Judge to Investigate Holdout Juror
item.description:
Lindsay Clancy’s defense lawyer has asked a Massachusetts judge to investigate the holdout juror in the murder case, which ended this month in a mistrial.

The motion from the lawyer, Kevin Reddington, dated on Friday, asks the judge, William Sullivan, to examine the juror’s mobile phone metadata during the time that the jury was deliberating over whether Ms. Clancy should be found guilty of murdering her three children.

It asks the court to preserve the original questionnaires for the deliberating jurors and alternates, and all the jury notes and the court’s responses.

It also asks the judge to examine the holdout juror on the record in front of lawyers, including asking him questions about the truthfulness of the information he provided during jury selection and the use of a phone or any other outside information during deliberations.

“The inquiry will not touch the substance of deliberations,” the motion said.

The motion doesn’t publicly seek a particular outcome from any investigation, though the defense filed additional documents under seal. It is unclear on what grounds the jury’s decision could be reversed.

“This able attorney is obligated to leave no stone unturned,” Jack Lu, a retired Massachusetts Superior Court judge, said by text Monday, referring to Mr. Reddington. Still, he said, undoing the mistrial would be a long shot.

Ms. Clancy, 36, did not deny strangling her children. Her lawyers argued that she had been in the grip of postpartum psychosis and mounted an insanity defense. The jurors were deciding whether she should be held criminally responsible and ultimately deadlocked, 11 to 1.

The holdout juror, Michael P. Desronvil, said on Friday that he had no doubts about Ms. Clancy’s guilt. He said in a statement that other jurors had repeatedly cut him off during deliberations when he tried to propound his theories of the case. He defended himself against accusations from some of the other jurors, who said he refused to follow the law regarding reasonable doubt.

Efforts to reach Mr. Desronvil’s lawyer were not immediately successful on Monday.

Valerie Hans, a law professor at Cornell University who studies juries, said Mr. Reddington’s motion “leaves a bad taste in your mouth.”

This kind of request typically happens only after a conviction, where the defense says that there was fraud, bribery or racist statements among jurors, she said.

The Clancy motion could signal to potential jurors “that privacy doesn’t matter if you come up with the wrong views in a case, views that the rest of the jury did not support,” Dr. Hans said.

After highly publicized debate about the hung jury in this trial and the latest motion, Dr. Hans said potential jurors may think, “Could I be in trouble? Could I have my phone taken from me and inspected?”

item.title: ICE Agents Encountered Austin Man by Chance Before Shooting Him
item.description:
The man shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Austin, Texas, on Sunday was not the target of a federal investigation before the encounter, according to two people familiar with the shooting.

ICE agents were in the area checking license plates when they discovered that the man, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela, had a deportation order on file, said the two people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak about the investigation.

ICE agents pulled Mr. Garces Perez over at about 12:45 p.m. while he was making DoorDash deliveries and told him they were ICE agents and that he was going to be arrested. Mr. Garces Perez fled in his car after that, the two people said.

A short chase ensued before ICE agents encountered Mr. Garces Perez again, they said. The shooting occurred after that. Mr. Garces Perez was shot in the torso and taken to an area hospital and later released into ICE custody. The Department of Homeland Security said he was in stable condition. He is being held at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, his lawyer said.

Mr. Garces Perez was being questioned at the processing center and has been denied pain medication for a bullet that remained lodged in his back, said Juan Proaño, the chief executive of the League of United Latin American Citizens, a Latino civil rights organization.

The shooting was the second in Texas by an ICE agent since July and the latest in a series of violent episodes involving federal immigration agents across the country. More than 20 people have been shot at by ICE since President Trump took office last year, nearly all of them in their cars, and some fatally.

D.H.S.’s Homeland Security Investigations, along with the Federal Bureau of Investigation, are leading the investigation into the shooting of Mr. Garces Perez, a spokesman for D.H.S. said.

Calls for an independent investigation have mounted following the encounter. Mayor Kirk Watson of Austin denounced the shooting at a news conference on Sunday. Representative Greg Casar, whose congressional district includes Austin, sent a letter to Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security, that called for the immediate release of unedited video footage, the sharing of all available evidence with local and state law enforcement, and urged officials to suspend the agent involved in the shooting and keep him in Austin until the investigation is done.

“D.H.S. has repeatedly lied about the facts following violent encounters involving agents and have blamed victims,” Mr. Casar wrote in his letter. “As a result, any narrative from D.H.S. regarding this shooting must be viewed with deep skepticism.”

Jose Garza, the district attorney for Travis County, which includes Austin, said his office and the Austin Police Department should be equal partners in the investigation and asked for the federal government to provide access to evidence gathered by D.H.S. and the F.B.I.

James Talarico, who is the Democratic nominee for Senate, also called for an independent investigation and the release of all video footage.

Videos of the shooting, which circulated on social media and were verified by The Times, captured audio of sirens blaring and tires screeching before the blue Toyota Corolla driven by Mr. Garces Perez and an unmarked Ford S.U.V. driven by a federal immigration officer were seen. Both vehicles were stopped and facing in opposite directions.

The videos show an officer exiting the driver’s side of the unmarked S.U.V. and circling around to the back passenger side of the Toyota. The immigration officer remains to the side of the vehicle as it rolls forward slightly.

Three gunshots can be heard, and the Toyota continues moving forward slowly before coming to a stop. The video then shows the officer running to the driver’s side of the vehicle.

Among those following the noise from the gunshots was a man who identified himself as Carlos, 60, who said he was a naturalized U.S. citizen but declined to give his last name out of fear of retaliation from authorities.

He said he approached the driver, who looked to be in pain. He then noticed a bullet wound on his back.

He said he asked Mr. Garces Perez if he was OK, and Mr. Garces Perez said yes but that he had been shot in the back. He added that Mr. Garces Perez said the officer shot him because he did not hit the brakes.

Edgar Sandoval and Lauren McGaughy contributed reporting.

item.title: Man Found Guilty of Shooting 3 Palestinian Students in Vermont
item.description:
The man charged with shooting three young men of Palestinian descent in 2023 in Burlington, Vt., was found guilty of three counts of attempted second-degree murder on Monday.

Lawyers for the man, Jason Eaton, 51, had argued that he was suffering from a delusional disorder at the time and believed that government agents had spoken to him through his radio and ordered him to shoot the men. The jury rejected their argument that Mr. Eaton was not criminally responsible for his actions because he was mentally ill.

The shootings, which took place two days after Thanksgiving, blocks from the bucolic campus of the University of Vermont, stunned residents of Burlington. The three victims, all 20-year-old college students at the time, were close friends spending the holiday weekend together at the Burlington home of one of their relatives.

Hisham Awartani, then a student at Brown University, was shot in the spine and paralyzed from the chest down. Tahseen Ali Ahmad, a student at Trinity College, was shot in the chest. Kinnan Abdalhamid, a student at Haverford College, was shot in the backside. The three had been friends since their childhood in the West Bank.

All three men testified in the trial last week, recounting what happened on Nov. 25, 2023. They were out for a walk around 6:30 p.m., talking in a mixture of English and Arabic. Two of the three were wearing kaffiyehs, traditional Palestinian scarves. Then Mr. Eaton appeared, pulled out a handgun and started shooting from about 10 feet away.

Prosecutors played audio of Mr. Awartani’s call to 911 minutes later, in which he told the dispatcher, “I think I’m going to die.”

Mr. Eaton’s mental health took center stage at the trial, similar to the recent trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother who strangled her three children in 2023. Lawyers for Ms. Clancy, 36, argued that she was not criminally responsible for her actions because she was experiencing postpartum psychosis and hallucinated a voice that ordered her to kill her children and herself.

At Ms. Clancy’s trial, in Plymouth, Mass., 11 of 12 jurors agreed that she was not criminally responsible. But one juror held out for conviction, leading to a mistrial after nearly 40 hours of deliberations.

Jurors in the Eaton trial deliberated for two hours before reaching a verdict.

At both trials, dueling psychiatric experts testified for the defense and prosecution and offered starkly different interpretations of the defendants’ symptoms. Dr. Fabian Saleh, a forensic psychiatrist testifying for the defense at Mr. Eaton’s trial, said that Mr. Eaton was suffering from an undiagnosed delusional disorder and “absolutely” did not understand the criminality of his conduct.

A forensic psychiatrist who testified for the prosecution disputed that Mr. Eaton was experiencing psychosis and said that he was not legally insane at the time of the shooting. The psychiatrist, Dr. Jhilam Biswas, said she had diagnosed him with substance use disorder because of excessive cannabis and alcohol use, which likely contributed to what she described as his extreme paranoia on the day of the shooting.

On Thursday, in the middle of his trial, Mr. Eaton asked the judge if he could fire his lawyers for failing to properly defend him. The judge denied his request.

Key to Mr. Eaton’s defense were audio recordings of a conversation he had with his lawyers days after the shootings, portions of which were played in court. In the recordings, he described hearing a cacophony of voices he believed were of C.I.A. agents — and at times, his grandfather — who ordered him to commit an act of violence to protect a Jewish family in his neighborhood.

He said the voices told him they needed his help because they were “stuck” in negotiations between Israel and Palestine. “They told me, it will cost you your life, but not to worry,” he said.

“There’s a chance I was the first human to be hacked,” Mr. Eaton said in the interview, before describing a final “crescendo” when the voices were “urging, urging, urging me.”

When he looked through his window and spotted the three young men walking down the street, he said, he went downstairs, shot them and returned to his apartment, where he waited for agents to rush in and kill him.

He described the series of events as “an out-of-body experience.”

“I still don’t know the answer,” he said. “Were they innocent victims? Were they planning an attack?”

Sarah George, the state’s attorney for Chittenden County, had been criticized for not prosecuting the shootings as a hate crime. Ms. George indicated that proving bias beyond a reasonable doubt would be difficult without “direct and great evidence” such as statements from Mr. Eaton.

In a statement days after the shooting, the families of the three victims rejected the claim that Mr. Eaton was not responsible for his actions and the suggestion that the shooting was not driven by hate.

“Millions of people in America and across the globe struggle with mental health challenges. That does not make them pick up a gun and attack people based on their identity,” they wrote. “We do not accept what this wrongfully implies about people who struggle with their mental health, nor do we accept it as justification or context for this heinous, hate-driven crime.”

At the trial, conflict erupted even before testimony began, when the judge, John Pacht, ordered spectators in the courtroom — including pro-Palestinian activists who were there to support the victims — to remove their kaffiyeh scarves, because of “concern about how that would impact the jury.”

The three victims of the shooting were allowed to wear their kaffiyehs in the courtroom.

item.title: Technical Problems Ground Flights at Major East Coast Airports
item.description:
At least five airports along the East Coast, including four that serve the New York region, experienced significant ground stops on Monday after a radio communications system in Philadelphia and its backup failed, triggering flight delays across one of the country’s most congested corridors.

By midafternoon, LaGuardia Airport, John F. Kennedy International Airport and Philadelphia International Airport had resumed delayed operations. But it was unclear when Newark Liberty International Airport and Teterboro Airport, a hub for private jets, would emerge from ground stops, after efforts to replace the radio communications module that failed were unsuccessful.The mounting delays and cancellations snarled hundreds of flights just as New York was welcoming world leaders for the United Nations General Assembly. Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada was forced to skip a summit and speech planned for Monday evening when the ground stops delayed his flight, according to a statement from his office.

More than 400 flights bound for affected airports in the Northeast had been canceled by Monday afternoon, according to FlightAware, while hundreds more had been delayed.

Bryan Bedford, who leads the Federal Aviation Administration, told reporters that the outages began Monday morning, when an antiquated communications circuit at a control center that manages flight traffic in the Philadelphia region failed, forcing Philadelphia and Newark to ground planes. At that point, he explained, controllers attempted to switch to a backup communications system that runs along fiber optic cable the F.A.A. recently installed as part of a push to modernize the air traffic control system.

But the backup was inoperable, Mr. Bedford said, because a 600-foot section of the fiber optic line had been cut, which officials only discovered after the main system failed.

“We didn’t know about the fiber break until after we lost the primary circuit,” he told reporters.

The damaged section of the fiber line was located between New Brunswick, N.J., and Newark, crippling the center’s ability to transmit radio and radar data, Mr. Bedford added.

In a statement, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said that the line had been cut by an Amtrak construction crew. In a statement, Verizon, which installed the fiber cable, said that the line runs adjacent to an Amtrak rail line, and that construction crews dug up and cut the cable. They did not specify when that happened, but said they were working to repair the cable — something Mr. Bedford said could take 13 hours.

As Verizon worked on repairing the fiber line, officials attempted to fix the initial failed circuit, Mr. Bedford — a fix that required them to suspend service to the New York area airports as well, to ensure that data could be safely transmitted.

But “the circuit replacement did not work,” Mr. Bedford said.

When asked if that meant that some flight traffic could be grounded until the fiber cable could be fully repaired, Mr. Bedford said he did not know.

Michael McCormick, a former air traffic controller and a professor of air traffic management at Embry‐Riddle Aeronautical University, said that the ground stops would likely lead to significant operational problems.

“They are not going to be able to recover today,” he said. “They are going to have crews, passengers and aircrafts in the wrong locations to start out their systems tomorrow morning. It may take them an additional two days to be able to recover.”

The incident, which unfolded as Mr. Bedford and Mr. Duffy were rolling out a new artificial intelligence tool to help air traffic controllers avoid delays, has revived concerns about the F.A.A.’s aging air traffic control infrastructure. Failures of that infrastructure have caused a number of outages in and around the New York region in recent years, which in turn have helped fuel urgent calls from Mr. Duffy and others to invest in modern upgrades.

But Monday’s ground stops raised new questions about whether the agency’s upgrades were durable enough.

“These are issues that aren’t new to us. We know these problems can happen. We know these cuts can happen,” Mr. Duffy told reporters. He said that fixing and modernizing the communications systems “all takes money,” and called on Congress to appropriate tens of billions of dollars more to help the department complete its work.

Mr. Bedford said that in a fully modernized system, the F.A.A. would rely on fiber optic cable as its main operating system, and have cloud-based services to function as backup. But those do not yet exist, he said.

Christine Chung and Ian Austen contributed reporting.

item.title: Two Killed in Helicopter Crash While Fighting Yosemite Wildfire
item.description:
Two people working on a contract for the U.S. Forest Service died on Sunday when their helicopter crashed while fighting a wildfire in Yosemite National Park, officials said.

The Federal Aviation Administration said the Eurocopter Super Puma helicopter crashed in Mariposa, Calif., at about 2:55 p.m. local time, while fighting the Dome fire, which has burned more than 3,200 acres since it started on Tuesday.

Only the two people were on board. Officials said the cause of the crash was under investigation.

The crew members worked for a private aviation company, Precision, which was under contract with the Forest Service, said Adrienne Freeman, a spokeswoman for the agency.

Data as of Sept. 21 at 7:32 p.m.. Source: Cal Fire William B. Davis, Madison Dong, Joel Eastwood and Joey K. Lee/The New York Times

At the time of the crash, they were engaged in “bucket work,” which involves scooping water out of a lake or river to dump on the fire, she said.

The Alaska Division of Forestry and Fire Protection identified one of the crew members as Greg King, a “cherished member of our wildland fire family,” who had deep ties to the agency, where close members of his family work. Officials did not release the name of the other crew member.

“Greg was a dedicated aviator and a dear friend to many of us,” the division said in a statement. “We are mourning both pilots who bravely supported firefighting efforts, and our hearts go out to their families. We are standing alongside our staff and Greg’s loved ones as we grieve this profound tragedy together.”

Precision confirmed in a statement that one of its helicopters had crashed on Sunday while “actively fighting the fire.”

“Currently we are respecting the families, friends and colleagues that are involved and connected to this tragic loss,” Precision, which is based in McMinnville, Ore., said. It added that “at the right time the families will share information that they feel is important for the broader public. This is a devastating loss to everyone involved.”

The National Transportation Safety Board confirmed it was investigating the crash, and said it would send investigators to the scene when fire conditions permitted.

A preliminary report on the crash will be released within 30 days, the agency said.

The Dome fire started last week about an hour’s drive south of Yosemite Valley, the most-visited section of Yosemite National Park.

More than 580 people are fighting the fire, which is 15 percent contained, according to Jay Nichols, a spokesman for the team coordinating the joint local, state and federal effort to control the blaze. The cause of the fire is unknown, he said.

Yosemite National Park said in a statement on Friday that although the park remained open, several trails had been closed and smoke was still visible as the fire continued to burn through brush, grass and timber.

The fire broke out during dry weather that is typical in the Sierra Nevada in the late summer. With little rain having fallen in recent months, the grass, brush and trees were parched and highly flammable.

item.title: Timothy Pigford, Who Fought Bias Against Black Farmers, Dies at 74
item.description:
Timothy Pigford, a North Carolina farmer whose lawsuit against the Department of Agriculture for systemically denying loans to Black farmers resulted in the largest civil rights settlement in U.S. history, died on Aug. 23 in Washington, N.C. He was 74.

His death, in a hospital, was confirmed by his wife, Janice Pigford, who said the cause was cancer.

Mr. Pigford was an embattled corn and soybean tenant farmer in southeastern North Carolina, tired of years of being turned down for loans by local white Agriculture Department officials, when he signed on with several other Black farmers to the landmark lawsuit Pigford v. Glickman in August 1997. The defendant was Dan Glickman, the U.S. secretary of agriculture.

The suit was an attempt to redress the department’s long history of racism, which the historian Evan Bennett said in an interview was “baked in from the beginning.” By some measures, Pigford v. Glickman was a big success.

The department had “willfully discriminated” in processing loan applications from 1983 to 1996, the suit said, though racism had festered for decades, particularly in the rural South, where agriculture officials were white, Jim Crow was the order of the day and Black farmers were losing their land at an alarming rate.

More than $2 billion was eventually doled out to tens of thousands of Black claimants, many in increments of $50,000, and Mr. Pigford and his wife got a handsome piece of it themselves in 2000, “one-point-something,” she recalled in an interview.

It seemed the end of a long struggle for Mr. Pigford and his wife, who had seen their electricity cut off, their house foreclosed on, their furniture thrown out in the yard and their crops destroyed by droughts and hurricanes.

Above all, he had triumphed over all the hostile white Agriculture Department officials in North Carolina who had told him for 25 years that he “didn’t have enough sense” to make it as a farmer, as he said to one interviewer in 1998, and had systematically denied him the loans he wanted to buy land.

But by the early 2010s, mostly what remained of the settlement was his name attached to the lawsuit. The settlement money was largely gone, siphoned away by back taxes, fines and loans gone bad. He was jobless and driving a car with 382,000 miles on it. His wife’s schoolteacher salary had been garnished.

“We were worse off than when we filed the lawsuit,” Mrs. Pigford said in the interview, adding that they were still, at her husband’s death, in debt for about $151,000. About the settlement, the I.R.S. “never told us how much of it was taxable,” she said.

The decline in the Pigfords’ fortunes coincided with a tarnishing of the lawsuit’s legacy, as the money went out and fraud claims surrounding the suit’s thousands of claimants piled up.

A 2013 New York Times investigation found, among other things, that in 16 ZIP codes in Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi and North Carolina, “the number of successful claimants exceeded the total number of farms operated by people of any race in 1997, the year the lawsuit was filed.”

In Little Rock, Ark., the Times investigation found, “10 members of one extended family collected a total of $500,000.”

There were other abuses and, for years, critics, and not just on the right, have faulted the government for its haste and sloppiness. Settlement negotiations in Pigford v. Glickman began a mere five months after the suit was filed, and little documentation for the discrimination claims was either available or produced.

The government agreed to settle after less than two years and, by 1999, it had paid more than $1 billion on nearly 16,000 claims, topped by another $1.25 billion in 2010 and 2011 for farmers who had filed claims too late the first time.

And yet Mr. Pigford’s stubbornness and his insistence — along with several other plaintiffs — that the agriculture agency be held accountable for its history of racism and discrimination, transcend the fraud findings, Mr. Bennett, the historian, suggested.

“His greatest legacy,” he wrote in an email, “was taking on an entrenched bureaucracy that refused to acknowledge its long history of denying Black farmers the same benefits it extended to white farmers.”

Other historians who specialize in the history of Black agriculture said they agree. “Mr. Pigford’s legacy is one of fighting for the U.S.D.A. to treat Black farmers equally, at great sacrifice to him and his family,” Adrienne Petty, a professor at the College of William and Mary, wrote in an email.

Timothy Charles Pigford was born in Willard, N.C., on Nov. 15, 1951, the son of Timothy Wright Pigford, a longshoreman, and May (Newkirk) Pigford. He was 4 when his father died and was raised on his grandfather’s farm, where he was farming by the time he was 8.

In 1969, the year he graduated from Penderlea High School, his wife said, he was president of the Future Farmers of America chapter (now National FFA Organization). He then attended the University of North Carolina Wilmington but did not graduate until coming back for his degree in 2013.

He began working at a local chemical plant and rented 25 acres to farm. In 1973, he began a long series of confrontations with the Farmers Home Administration, the Agriculture Department’s now-defunct local agency.

He had asked for a loan of $47,000 to buy 100 acres of farmland but was turned down when he couldn’t come up with a required 10 percent, according to the 2021 book “Just Harvest: The Story of How Black Farmers Won the Largest Civil Rights Case Against the U.S. Government,” by Greg Francis.

For several years thereafter, Mr. Pigford was able to obtain loans to rent land but never to buy it, according to Mr. Francis. In 1976, tired of being a tenant, Mr. Pigford again asked Farmers Home for a loan of $110,000 to buy 170 acres. “I had my heart set on buying that farm,” he later told the magazine Business North Carolina. He was turned down.

In September 1984, Mr. Pigford, who had increasingly become a steadfast advocate for North Carolina’s Black farmers, described to a congressional subcommittee on civil and constitutional rights the plight of Black farmers and their lack of access to credit.

“President Lincoln gave to Blacks after the Civil War 40 acres and a mule,” Mr. Pigford told the congressmen, “and at the present rate that Blacks are losing land today, we have lost the mule and almost lost the 40 acres.”

After his testimony, “all hell broke loose,” his wife recalled, and the county supervisor in Bladen County told him he wouldn’t get another loan “unless Jesse Helms himself,” the powerful senior senator from North Carolina, requested it. He filed his first discrimination complaint with the Agriculture Department shortly after.

Serious problems for the Pigford household ensued — indebtedness, foreclosure, eviction, dispossession.

By the 1990s, Mr. Pigford was well acquainted with the staff of the North Carolina congressman Charlie Rose; one staffer connected him with a growing band of lawyers and Black farmer activists.

The atmosphere was ripe: In December 1996, Black farmers demonstrated outside the White House demanding equal treatment. In response, Mr. Glickman established what he called a “civil rights action team” to listen to complaints across the country in the new year. There were marches in Washington, Atlanta and elsewhere.

The allegations of discrimination that echoed forth were all familiar to Mr. Pigford, who soon lent his name to the lawsuit.

He is survived by his wife — they were married in 1975 — and two sons, Timothy Jr. and Cornelius.

For Mr. Pigford, the lawsuit was never just about his own struggle, Mrs. Pigford said.

“He had found out about all the other, similar stories,” she said. “It was injustice. He didn’t want other people to suffer what we had went through.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: What We Know About the ICE Shooting in Austin, Texas
item.description:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent shot an immigrant from Venezuela in his vehicle on Sunday afternoon in Austin, Texas. It was the latest in a series of violent encounters between agents and people in cars as the Trump administration continues its immigration crackdown.

The man, Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, who was shot in the torso, was taken to a nearby hospital and later released into ICE custody.

Mr. Garces Perez said at a news conference on Monday that a bullet lodged near his spine was not removed because ICE agents were in a hurry to move him out of the hospital.

He is being held and questioned at an ICE processing facility in Texas, his lawyer said.

“I am not doing well because of the gunshot wound I received,” Mr. Garces Perez said in Spanish. “I have not received the necessary medical attention.”

His lawyer said that Mr. Garces Perez entered the country legally in 2024.

The shooting was the second in Texas by an ICE agent in recent months. Since September, more than 20 people have been fired on by ICE across the country, some fatally. Nearly all were in their vehicles.

Mayor Kirk Watson of Austin said at a news conference on Sunday that he was “very angry” but “not surprised.”

“It’s happened in other cities,” he said, “with the nature of ICE and the way ICE is doing its business these days and the chaos that we see it performing and fomenting.”

Here’s what we know.

On Sunday afternoon, ICE agents were checking license plates in northwest Austin, where Mr. Garces Perez was making DoorDash deliveries, when they discovered that he had a deportation order on file, two people familiar with the incident said.

Around 12:45 p.m., the agents pulled Mr. Garces Perez over and told him they were going to arrest him. Mr. Garces Perez fled in his car, leading to chase, the two people said.

A few minutes later, Mr. Garces Perez’s blue Toyota Corolla and an unmarked Ford SUV were stopped beneath a highway overpass, facing opposite directions, when an officer exited the SUV and approached Mr. Garces Perez’s car, videos posted on social media and verified by The Times show.

As Mr. Garces Perez’s Toyota inched forward, the officer remained standing to the side of the vehicle. Three gunshots rang out and the car rolled forward slightly before stopping.

Mr. Garces Perez’s wife, Elizdar, said in an interview that he called her from the driver’s seat, crying and saying he was in pain.

When Mr. Garces Perez was removed from his vehicle and placed in handcuffs, footage shows, he was applying pressure to his left shoulder. A wound in his upper back appeared to bleed as officers sat him down on the curb.

By the time that Mr. Garces Perez’s wife arrived at the scene, her husband had been transported to a nearby hospital, where she was not permitted to see him, she said.

Mr. Garces Perez is now being held at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, according to his lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.

More than 200 protesters assembled at the site of the shooting on Sunday and remained there for several hours, waving Mexican flags and chanting through bullhorns through the evening.

The Department of Homeland Security’s investigations unit and the Federal Bureau of Investigation are leading the investigation into the shooting of Mr. Garces Perez, a spokesman for D.H.S. said.

Representative Greg Casar, whose congressional district includes the area of the shooting, called for an independent investigation in a letter sent to Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary.

“D.H.S has repeatedly lied about the facts following violent encounters involving agents and have blamed victims,” Mr. Casar wrote. “As a result any narrative from D.H.S regarding this shooting must be viewed with deep skepticism.”

The letter also calls for the immediate release of unedited video footage of the incident, the sharing of all available evidence with local and state law enforcement and for the agent involved in the shooting to be suspended and remain in Austin while the investigation is resolved.

James Talarico, who is the Democratic nominee for Senate, also called for an independent investigation and the release of all video footage.

The shooting is one of several in recent months involving victims who may not have been the initial targets of immigration agents.

In July, an ICE agent in Houston shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo while he was on his way to work at a construction site in his vehicle with three other men.

Federal officials later said that he had not been the operation’s intended target.

Less than a week later, an ICE agent shot and killed another man headed to work in Biddeford, Maine.

Six of the more than 20 people who have been fired on by federal immigration agents since Mr. Trump took office in January 2025 have been killed, including three U.S. citizens.

item.title: Worker at Los Angeles Senior Home Shoots 3 Colleagues, Police Say
item.description:
A staff member at a senior living center in South Los Angeles opened fire in the lobby of the building on Monday, injuring three other employees, one of them critically, before he was taken into custody, the police said.

The shooting, at the Progressive Home for the Elderly, was reported just before 11 a.m., Deputy Chief Marc Reina of the Los Angeles police said at a news conference. Officers were at the scene within two minutes, and when a suspect was not immediately located, the call was upgraded to a “possible active shooter” situation, Chief Reina said.

The center was placed on lockdown and the police conducted a full sweep of the building, where more than 100 seniors live. Chief Reina said officers found the suspect on a different floor of the building but could not confirm which one.

The suspect, who is in his 60s, was not immediately charged. He shot three colleagues — a woman in her 40s, a woman in 70s and a man in his 60s, Chief Reina said. The victims were taken to a hospital, where one was in critical condition and the others were stable, he said.

Chief Reina said the gunman was taken into custody without incident. The police did not say what job he held at the senior living center.

The swift police response “prevented further injury or loss of life of this very precious population,” Marqueece Harris-Dawson, the president of the Los Angeles City Council, said at the news conference.

Dorothy Mobley, a caregiver, told KTLA that she was checking in at the front desk to visit a client when the gunman opened fire. She said she recognized him as a custodian in the building.

He said, “I’m tired of this,” and pulled out a gun and started shooting, Ms. Mobley said. She then ran outside.

“I never would have expected that,” she said. “He’s a nice guy, he don’t bother anybody or anything.”

item.title: Hunter Mistook Woman for Deer in Fatal Delaware Shooting, Police Say
item.description:
A hunter is facing a manslaughter charge in Delaware in the fatal shooting of a woman whom he mistook for a deer while she crossed an open field with three other people, the authorities said.

The man, Walter W. Moorhead, 74, fired his rifle from a ground blind, a tent, shed or other makeshift structure used by hunters to conceal themselves, when he struck Santos Maria Chilel Soto, 39, on a private property on Friday night in Ellendale, Del., the Delaware State Police said.

Investigators said the shooting occurred around 7:40 p.m., just over 30 minutes after sunset, in an area dotted with farms, about 75 miles south of Wilmington, Del., and west of Delaware’s well-known coastal resorts.

Ms. Soto, who a GoFundMe page said was a mother of five from Guatemala, was with her boyfriend and her boyfriend’s two children when she was shot, according to an arrest warrant. It was not clear why Ms. Soto, who lived in Georgetown, Del., was on the property.

The victim’s boyfriend told the police that the four of them had been walking together across the field when he heard an explosion and saw Ms. Soto fall to the ground with a gunshot wound to her torso, the warrant said.

An older white man, whom investigators identified as Mr. Moorhead, approached with a flashlight to search for the deer he thought he had shot, Detective M. Csapo of the Delaware State Police wrote in the warrant.

During an interview with the police, the authorities said, Mr. Moorhead acknowledged that he had struck Ms. Soto.

Mr. Moorhead, of Salisbury, Md., was also charged with three counts of reckless endangering and possession of a firearm during the commission of a felony. He was released on a $43,000 cash bond.

Efforts to reach Mr. Moorhead were not immediately successful on Monday. It was not clear if had a lawyer.

Mr. Moorhead had been hunting under what is known in Delaware as a crop damage permit, Cpl. Raushan Rich of the Delaware State Police said in an email on Monday.

The program allows commercial farms that experience crop damage to hunt antlerless deer, specifically mature does, more frequently than under normal deer hunting regulations.

The state, which expanded the program this year, allows deer hunting from a half-hour before sunrise until a half-hour after sunset, which was about 7:06 p.m. on Friday in Ellendale.

In Delaware, the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control oversees hunting regulations. It did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Monday or provide a copy of the hunting permit associated with the farm where the shooting occurred.

Details about who owns the property were also not immediately available.

In a Facebook post on Saturday, Iglesia de Dios Fuente de Verdad Delaware in Georgetown announced Ms. Soto’s death. Organizers of the GoFundMe page were seeking donations to help return Ms. Soto’s body to Guatemala.

item.title: The State of the Economy Before the Midterms: Rising Inflation and A.I. Unease
item.description:
Six weeks before the midterm elections, the cost of living is steadily marching upward.

The price of gas has risen to a national average of $4.47 a gallon, up 41 percent since this time last year. The price of diesel fuel has reached a record high. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates last week for the first time in three years; mortgage rates have reached their highest level in more than a year.

Politically speaking, these figures are deeply alarming to Republicans as Democrats try to turn the November election into a referendum on affordability. Polling tells us that voters view the economy as their top issue this fall — and the economy right now is, well, weird.

Tonight, I want to sidestep the political spin and break down what’s really happening with the economy and the cost of living. Lucky for all of us, I’m not trying to do this on my own. I asked The Times’s chief economics correspondent, Ben Casselman, to guide us.

The bottom line: “Broadly speaking,” he said, “the economy is not too bad, but the affordability issues that everybody is so worried about have gotten significantly worse.”

When President Trump talks about the economy, he has pointed to a set of robust metrics, including the unemployment rate and the stock market, to insist that he has a success story to tell. It’s true, Ben says, that these longtime indicators of economic health look pretty decent. They’re just not the whole story.

The labor force: The unemployment rate right now is 4.1 percent. That’s pretty low, and it means that most people who want a job have one — in part because aging and the immigration crackdown have stemmed the growth of the labor force. But job growth is low, too, and it’s pretty tough out there for young people.

Wage growth: This has been OK — but it has been slowing this year, and it’s not keeping pace with inflation.

The stock market: Major stock indexes have been setting records in recent years. If you make most of your money from the stock market, you’re probably feeling good. The boom has been fueled by investor enthusiasm for anything connected to A.I. — but there are big questions about what happens if that confidence wilts.

Consumer spending: Americans are spending big, Ben told me, in part because of the windfall from the stock market. As prices rise, though, many people are stretching more to keep up their spending.

So, is spending dropping and unemployment rising, as it does in a recession? No! But a big part of what’s driving the economy is investment in A.I. — and if you strip that away, the underlying economy isn’t so strong. This has created a great deal of uncertainty about where the economy is going, Ben said:

“If A.I. succeeds, then it may kill all of our jobs. If it fails, then the whole economy falls apart, and your 401(k) blows up, and maybe you still lose your job. You can kind of understand why maybe people aren’t super enthusiastic about the state of things.”

We know that people don’t vote based on economic indicators. They vote based on how the economy feels to them — and that’s usually a question of the cost of living. (Just ask the Democrats in 2024.)

Inflation: The war with Iran has driven up the cost of fuel, making it more expensive to buy stuff. This indicator is nowhere near the high of 2022 — but, after seeming to come under control, inflation picked up again this year, prompting the Fed, led by Trump’s handpicked chairman, Kevin Warsh, to raise interest rates last week.

The cost of living: Affordability challenges go beyond consumer prices. Because of the interest rate increase, it’s also getting more expensive to borrow money for a car loan, or just on your credit card. (The bond market has been going haywire, too, which has driven mortgage rates higher.)

“Every piece of this affordability issue,” Ben said, “is getting worse rather than getting better.”

Catch Me Up

The three news organizations that Trump barred from the White House last week — CNN, MS Now and Politico — sued to overturn his order. Major TV networks (including Fox News) agreed to suspend their shared coverage of the president in protest.

Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery resolved an antitrust lawsuit that had stood in the way of their Hollywood mega-merger. The deal would make members of the Ellison family, who are close Trump allies, some of the most powerful figures in entertainment.

Trump met with Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York today. Republicans have been seeking to make the mayor the face of the political left ahead of the midterms, but Trump spoke warmly of Mamdani after their meeting.

Representative Jared Golden, a conservative Democrat who is not running for re-election, angered party leaders when he crossed the aisle to endorse Representative Mike Lawler, a New York Republican facing a tough race.

I wrote recently about how A.I. was shaking up this election. It seems to be already shaking up the next election, too, as 2028 hopefuls rush to figure out — or change — their stance on the fast-developing technology. Here are a few:

Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania. Shapiro, a Democrat, was an early champion of A.I. data centers, but he backtracked after that proved to be a political albatross. He says the government should require third-party oversight of A.I. but he opposes an outright pause on development.

Gov. Gavin Newsom of California. Newsom, a Democrat whose state is home to many A.I. companies, last week ordered the state to strengthen its A.I. safety laws. That represents a flip for the governor, who two years ago vetoed an A.I. safety bill with provisions similar to those he now supports.

Vice President JD Vance. He has largely echoed Trump, who vehemently opposes new regulations. Vance said last week, “If you’re going to create Frankenstein, don’t come to the government and say, ‘We need regulation.’”

Senator Ted Cruz. The Texas Republican called for “substantially more regulation” of A.I but said a full pause on development, or even slowing it down, would be a bad idea.

Number of the Day

That’s how much more Republicans and their allies are currently poised to spend on advertising than their Democratic counterparts, according to new data from the media tracking firm AdImpact. The total includes spending on Senate, House and state races.

As we approach Election Day, there are scads of interesting new polls coming out every day. I asked Ruth Igielnik, The Times’s polling editor, to highlight three that caught her eye.

An NBC News poll released over the weekend found that Americans would prefer Democrats to control Congress after the November election. The poll also found that Democrats had expanded their advantage on the most important issue, the economy.

A Fox News poll underlined just how much economic concerns are driving voters toward the Democratic Party. Two-thirds of all voters, and even one-quarter of Republicans, said the Trump administration had made the economy worse.

The Washington Post and George Mason University are out with a poll in Michigan showing the Senate race there to be neck-and-neck, with Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat, holding a slight edge. Still, the poll was a mixed bag for Democrats. The share of Black voters in the state who want Democrats to control the Senate (83 percent) was far greater than the share who planned to vote for El-Sayed (67 percent) — a sign the candidate might be running behind the rest of his party.

You can find much more on The Times’s poll tracker, which updates daily with new polls from across the country.

In the Comments

My colleague Reid Epstein answered readers’ questions in the comments on his recent story about Republicans’ midterm woes.

Do attack ads actually do anything? Who is swayed by a commercial to change their moral compass?

@Zep Strategists widely see them as effective, which is why screens are flooded with them before every competitive election. Ads from both parties tend to be targeted not at people who are avid politics followers or even regular New York Times readers, but at voters who only casually pay attention to politics if they do at all. There is evidence that political advertising – especially negative ads – sways opinion and can change the outcome of close elections.

ONE LAST THING

In an interview on “CBS Mornings” today, Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois revealed that he had dropped 80 pounds since he began taking GLP-1 weight-loss drugs in 2024.

There is a long history of elected officials — Chris Christie, Jeb Bush and Cory Booker, to name a few — getting in better shape before a presidential run. But Pritzker, a Democrat, is keeping his cards close to his chest for now.

“I have not made any decisions about what I might do in the future,” Pritzker said. “I can tell you, I want to be the governor of the state of Illinois for a while longer.”

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Appeals Court Sides With Missouri Republicans on Redrawn House Map
item.description:
The fight over Missouri’s congressional map took another confusing turn on Monday as a federal appellate panel sided with Republicans who want the general election to be held using boundaries redrawn to favor their party.

But because of a previous U.S. Supreme Court decision, Missouri is still set for now to hold its general election under the map used in the 2022 and 2024 elections. The Supreme Court has already cleared the way twice for the older map to be used in November, and ballots were required to be mailed to overseas and military voters last week. The ruling on Monday, from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, was likely to place the question back before the justices.

Nearly a quarter of the state's registered voters are assigned to different districts in the general election than they were in the primary.

Note: District lines shown are those expected to be used in the November general election.

Sources: New York Times analysis of voter registration data compiled by L2 (number of affected voters); United States Census Bureau (roads and populated areas).

Leanne Abraham and Irineo Cabreros/The New York Times

The decision cast fresh doubt on whether the eventual winners of those elections would be seated in Congress. The state’s primary was held last month using the redrawn boundaries, creating a rare situation in which many voters would be casting ballots for general election candidates whom they had no say in nominating.

Whatever happens now, officials from both parties have acknowledged, post-election lawsuits seem likely.

The Eighth Circuit panel, composed of three judges nominated by Republican presidents, said that “Missouri’s current plan to use the 2022 map in the November 2026 general election violates the Constitution.”

Still, the appellate court ordered a federal district judge to give the Supreme Court a week to review the issue, leaving continued uncertainty over which map will be used.

The panel was hearing an appeal in a case filed by Republican congressional candidates who wanted to use the redrawn map in the general election. Using one set of lines in the primary and another in November, the candidates argued, would be unconstitutional.

Officials with the offices of the governor, attorney general and secretary of state in Missouri did not immediately reply to requests for comment.

The leader of People Not Politicians Missouri, an anti-redistricting group that has sought a statewide vote on the new map, said he would file an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.

“Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections,” said the leader, Richard von Glahn.

Missouri was among several states that redrew congressional maps outside the usual once-a-decade cycle, prompted by President Trump’s demand last summer. But while other states’ boundaries have been settled for months, Missouri’s have remained murky.

Republicans now hold six of Missouri’s eight U.S. House seats. The redrawn map, which legislators approved last year during a special session, would position Republicans to flip a Kansas City-area district now held by Democrats, which could help determine control of Congress.

Redistricting opponents gathered hundreds of thousands of signatures seeking a statewide vote on the new map, leading to uncertainty over which lines were in effect.

On Primary Day, Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, said he believed redistricting was not eligible for a referendum. The Missouri Supreme Court disagreed, saying the redrawn boundaries were not yet law, and ordered the question to appear on the November ballot. By then, candidates had already campaigned and voters had already cast primary ballots under the redrawn lines.

The state Supreme Court ruling set off a series of confusing and sometimes contradictory court orders that left many county election officials and voters baffled.

That does not mean the fight is over. Officials from both parties have predicted that losing candidates could challenge the general election results in court.

“I’m sure there will be some lawsuits” if the older map is used, Mr. Hoskins said in an interview this month.

Reporting was contributed by Leanne Abraham, Irineo Cabreros and Ann E. Marimow.

item.title: Bush and Cornyn Leave Out Paxton as They Raise Cash for Senate Candidates
item.description:
Former President George W. Bush and Senator John Cornyn, two top Texas Republicans, are rallying conservative donors behind the party’s Senate candidates — except for the one running in their own state, Ken Paxton.

Mr. Cornyn is hosting a fund-raiser on Monday evening in Dallas for six Republican nominees in battleground states, according to an invitation to the event that was obtained by The New York Times. Mr. Bush, listed on the invite as a “special guest,” is attending the event, his spokesman confirmed.

The event will benefit Maintain the Majority, a new joint fund-raising committee supporting the Senate candidates, who are defending Republican-held seats in Maine, Ohio, Alaska and Iowa and looking to flip seats in Michigan and New Hampshire.

But Mr. Paxton, the Republican nominee in Texas, who defeated Mr. Cornyn in a costly and bitter primary, was not included. His campaign declined to comment on the fund-raiser.

The fund-raising omission of Mr. Paxton is another escalation in the standoff between old-guard Bush Republicans and the fiery insurgent wing represented by the party’s Senate nominee, Mr. Paxton, President Trump and their allies.

And it comes as the parties battle for cash and advertising time in the Texas Senate race, one of this year’s top contests. Mr. Paxton has badly trailed his Democratic opponent, James Talarico, in campaign fund-raising, but super PACs tied to Mr. Trump and Senate Republicans have come to Mr. Paxton’s aid, reserving more than $80 million in outside advertising in Texas.

Mr. Paxton, the state attorney general, has long been a polarizing figure among Texas Republicans. He was impeached by the Republican-dominated Texas House on corruption charges in 2023, though he was acquitted in the State Senate, and he pushed to oust Republican lawmakers and judges who disagreed with him in his party’s primaries in 2024.

This year, Mr. Cornyn and establishment Republican donors spent more than $130 million on advertising backing the senator and bashing Mr. Paxton in their contentious primary. (Mr. Bush chipped in $5,000 for Mr. Cornyn.) In the months since, Mr. Cornyn has continually criticized Mr. Paxton’s character and campaign.

“Paxton’s a poor campaigner,” Mr. Cornyn told The Texas Tribune in August. “He’s lazy and doesn’t raise money. And he basically is not offering a very compelling case for his election. He’s making this harder than it needs to be.” (Mr. Paxton countered the attacks, saying on Fox News’s “The Sunday Briefing” that “John Cornyn doesn’t know my schedule. He doesn’t know how many hours I’m putting in every day, 18 hours a day.” )

The fund-raiser comes as long-simmering tensions between Bush- and Trump-era Texas factions burst to the surface.

Last week, Karl Rove, Mr. Bush’s former senior adviser, announced that he would not vote for Bo French, the Republican nominee for the Texas state agency that regulates oil and gas, because of a racist social media post by Mr. French. Mr. Paxton declined to condemn Mr. French’s post, and Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social that Mr. Rove was a “stone-cold loser.”

Mr. Paxton has attacked Mr. Rove in the past, including in an interview with the conservative pundit Tucker Carlson in 2023.

Mr. Paxton has also gone head-to-head with a scion of the Bush dynasty, soundly defeating Mr. Bush’s nephew, George P. Bush, in the 2022 Republican primary for Texas attorney general. And Mr. Paxton has long criticized Mr. Cornyn for his willingness to work with Democrats on bipartisan legislation.

The host committee of the Monday fund-raiser includes paragons of the Bush-era Republican Party like Harriet Miers, Mr. Bush’s onetime nominee for the U.S. Supreme Court; former Senator Kay Bailey Hutchison; and the Republican megadonor Harlan Crow.

One of the candidates the event seeks to support is John E. Sununu, the Republican nominee for Senate in New Hampshire. His father, also named John Sununu, served as the White House chief of staff for Mr. Bush’s father, George H.W. Bush. Contributions ranging between $1,000 and $61,500 are required for entry, according to the invitation.

Some of the donors invited to the event on Monday have also contributed to Mr. Paxton’s campaign.

The gathering and the new fund-raising committee will benefit Senators Susan Collins of Maine, Jon Husted of Ohio and Dan Sullivan of Alaska, who are defending their seats in competitive general-election races, as well as three other Senate candidates: Mr. Sununu, Representative Ashley Hinson of Iowa and former Representative Mike Rogers of Michigan.

Ms. Collins “appreciates the support of Senator Cornyn and President Bush,” said Blake Kernen, a spokeswoman for Ms. Collins’s campaign. Representatives for the other candidates did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

item.title: After Years as the Star of Must-See TV, Trump Faces the Sting of Cancellation
item.description:
For President Trump, this is the tree-falls-in-the-forest moment of his administration. If the most television-addicted president in history suddenly finds the cameras missing, is he really still president? Not the kind he has been, anyway.

Mr. Trump, for whom television is better than any narcotic, finds himself for the first time at least partially deprived of the major networks that have covered nearly every movement and utterance he has made for more than a decade. No longer can he snap his fingers and appear live in millions of homes. No longer does he totally dominate the airwaves.

Indeed, his first taste of life without the major television networks that are now boycotting the White House press pool in protest of his ban on select news outlets was a sour one. He was left almost literally shouting into the wind on Monday as he cut the ribbon on his new helipad on the South Lawn of the White House, recorded only by a second-tier news broadcaster that could not capture his voice over the roar of Marine One. There was Mr. Trump moving his mouth, and no one could hear him.

Yet when it comes to attracting attention, the president still manages to find a way. By the end of the day, there he was live on CNN and Fox News after all — not filmed by the White House television pool, which refused to follow him, but by other cameras that met him when he arrived in New York. He had to rely on Mayor Zohran Mamdani to get on air, not at his own White House but as a guest at Gracie Mansion in the heart of liberal America. He crowed that he could still force his way onto the screen.

“They said they’re going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn’t very worried about that,” Mr. Trump boasted with the mayor at his side and a large group of reporters in front of him. “Look at all that press.”

The moment reinforced the challenge of carrying out any kind of television blackout on the president in an age of proliferating media, and the limits of the news industry’s self discipline. But the walkout by the five major networks that follow the president everywhere he goes still represents a threat to the way Mr. Trump has governed.

Television has been central to his rise to fame and power. His 14 seasons on reality television made him into a national force and helped propel him to the White House. His 10 seasons on political television since then have allowed him to dominate American life in a way that none of his predecessors ever did.

“This is the most important thing for Trump,” said Ramin Setoodeh, the author of “Apprentice in Wonderland,” a history of Mr. Trump’s career on reality TV. “When I interviewed him for my book, he told me the only thing that matters is ratings. It doesn’t matter if you’re a good person or a bad person. If you have good ratings, you’re successful.”

So to lose the network cameras, even if just for now and even if he can get around it some of the time, is a blow to his sense of self, Mr. Setoodeh said. “To him, this is equal to being canceled. This is equal to having a hit show and having the networks pull it from the lineup.”

“This is a real crisis for the president,” Mr. Setoodeh added.

The crisis, of course, is one of his making, stemming from his abrupt decision to bar CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House grounds because of their “negative” coverage, a prohibition he himself called a “ban on the free press.” The five networks that make up the rotating pool that provides television coverage of the president’s events — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC — decided to stop filming him, to demonstrate their objections.

The showdown could be resolved soon if a lawsuit filed by the three barred outlets finds quick favor in court. The case was assigned to Judge Timothy J. Kelly, a Trump appointee who ordered the White House to restore press credentials to CNN’s Jim Acosta during Mr. Trump’s first term. The judge scheduled a hearing for Wednesday, and Mr. Trump seemed to anticipate losing, announcing on social media that he would appeal even though no ruling had been issued.

Mr. Trump was clear that his decision was based on nothing more than his personal pique. “Virtually every story about me, or anything having to do with me, is negative, wrong and, in many cases, DANGEROUS for our Country!” he complained on social media. “No matter how GREAT my Achievements, they trivialize and demean.”

The White House did not comment on how it would respond to the absence of the major networks, but few expected Mr. Trump to take their disappearance with equanimity.

“Attention is Trump’s oxygen,” said Mark McKinnon, who was a media consultant for President George W. Bush and Senator John McCain, Republican of Arizona. “And there is no greater attention magnet and magnifier than television. So it is hard to imagine Donald Trump content for very long to have his main source of energy unplugged.”

The fact that the helipad ribbon-cutting would be the first moment when Mr. Trump would pay the price of his decision was especially rich. He has been exceedingly proud of his construction projects and relishes showing them off. Indeed, he has displayed the helipad more than once already, bursting with glee about its virtues. Not having the network cameras present for the big unveiling had to sting.

The only television cameras that did show up were from the White House itself, and less prominent outlets, such as Newsmax. The video was instantly mocked because of the bad sound. Even a Newsmax anchor said on air that the episode indicated that the president’s media ban was “backfiring just a little bit.”

“He’s got to be furious there’s no video with good audio from a consequential day,” said Alyssa Farah Griffin, who was Mr. Trump’s White House communications director in his first term, before breaking with him. “He doesn’t see the value of doing things other than for the camera.”

She added that she would “hate to be that staffer to tell him” what had happened with the ribbon-cutting.

Mr. Trump then flew to New York for the opening of the U.N. General Assembly, and met first with Mr. Mamdani. None of the major networks traveled with him on Air Force One, nor were they planning to be present at his meetings with foreign counterparts over the next day. If the dispute remains unresolved, Mr. Trump will return to Washington to host Xi Jinping, China’s leader, on Wednesday and Thursday without network cameras present.

“As far as I know, there is no precedent either for a president to ban cameras or networks — or for networks to boycott an event in solidarity with their banned colleagues,” said Harold Holzer, the author of “The Presidents vs. the Press” and the director of the Roosevelt House Public Policy Institute at Hunter College. “I was waiting for that to happen but honestly despaired of it. Thrilled to see it.”

While some presidents were also obsessed with television — Lyndon B. Johnson famously had a custom-made cabinet with three sets in the Oval Office so he could watch all of the network evening newscasts simultaneously — few have craved its attention, or benefited from it, as much as Mr. Trump.

Some even made a point of not checking it out personally, to avoid getting angry. Mr. Bush told television reporters that he did not watch their broadcasts, including even his daughter, Jenna Bush Hager, a host on NBC’s “Today” show. “He says things like, ‘I don’t watch your dumb show,’” she once revealed. Barack Obama tuned into ESPN’s “SportsCenter” religiously, but not the news networks. “I have not watched cable news in 15 years,” he said last year.

Not Mr. Trump. When he first arrived in the White House, he installed a 60-inch screen in the dining room off the Oval Office, along with a DirecTV Genie HD DVR that he called his “Super TiVo,” because it let him record multiple shows at once. He kept the television on throughout much of the day, even during meetings — with the sound down. When The New York Times reported in his first year in office that he watched at least four hours a day, he angrily denied it. But some close to him later suggested that the number underestimated his screen consumption.

Mr. Trump loves television so much that one former aide compared him to Mike Teavee, the television-obsessed kid in Roald Dahl’s classic children’s book who persuades Willy Wonka to transport him into a television set. Mr. Trump thinks about lighting and angles so much that he has been known to study iPad images of himself before starting a television interview, to check the best camera position. He prefers to be seen from his right side so that the part in his hair does not show.

Television is also how his allies communicate with him. Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died in July, often said that if he needed to get through to the president, he would appear on Sean Hannity’s show on Fox News, knowing that the president would see. A current cabinet secretary confided to a former Republican official that his best chance to talk directly with Mr. Trump comes during the phone call that reliably follows a television appearance.

In Mr. Trump’s view, television has worked well for him. He was such a master of the medium that in his first campaign, cable networks would air live images of an empty podium waiting for him to appear. Producers knew that he would say something provocative, and that ratings were good.

But the ratings are not what they once were. When Mr. Trump headlined a midterm Republican convention this month, he boasted that “the overall numbers beat the NFL.” In fact, only three million viewers tuned in to Mr. Trump’s speech the first night, compared with 25 million who watched the Seattle Seahawks edge past the New England Patriots.

With the networks on the sidelines, the White House tried to compensate by promoting its own live feed online, essentially a form of state television. “Get real-time updates and live events streamed DIRECTLY to your phone,” it wrote on social media. “No noise. Just the news that matters most — straight from the Trump Administration.”

Mr. Trump, of course, is all about the noise. And when he turns on his television and does not see his helipad or other events, the question is what kind of noise he will make then.

item.title: Princeton’s Run Atop U.S. News Rankings Ends After 15 Years
item.description:
Princeton University is no longer No. 1.

U.S. News & World Report, which had put Princeton atop its college rankings for 15 years, announced Tuesday that the Massachusetts Institute of Technology had seized the top spot.

How much it matters — or should — is contentious since U.S. News, like all publishers of college rankings, relies on an arbitrary, shifting formula to measure schools. But history suggests that the biggest consequence of Princeton’s dip to No. 2 may well be limited to grumbling among alumni.

U.S. News said M.I.T. had top showings in metrics related to faculty research, standardized test scores among incoming students and how much students earn after graduation.

“Princeton’s underlying rankings data netted out about the same,” Eric Brooks, U.S. News’s director of education data analysis, said in an email. “But the gap between Princeton and other universities had narrowed over the past few editions since we added faculty research metrics.”

In a statement, M.I.T. did not comment directly to its new ranking but said it was “part of a strong network of excellent colleges and universities across the nation, dedicated to educating students and pursuing curiosity-driven research.”

Princeton declined to comment, though it has not defined its relevance around U.S. News’s lists. Almost five years ago, Princeton’s president, Christopher L. Eisgruber, blistered the college rankings “game” as “a slightly daft obsession that does harm when colleges, parents, or students take it too seriously.”

But it has been big business for U.S. News, which started its rankings in 1983 and has made millions of dollars by licensing its name and logo to colleges. This year, the publisher said, it ranked more schools than ever.

Among national universities, Harvard and Yale held their respective No. 3 and 4 rankings as the California Institute of Technology and Stanford tied for fifth.

Private schools took the top 19 places before the University of California’s campuses in Berkeley and Los Angeles tied as the country’s leading public institutions. Williams College held onto its claim as U.S. News’s pick for best national liberal arts college, just like Spelman College retained its top ranking among historically Black schools.

U.S. News, which last published its newsmagazine in 2010, defends its rankings as a consumer service that draws more than 100 million annual visitors to its website. Surveys suggest, though, that the rankings are not influential as they once were, as students and parents have increasingly easy access to information about schools from other sources.

College administrators often privately castigate the rankings as merely one publisher’s subjective view, no matter how enrobed they are in weighted statistics. In some instances, schools have refused to respond to U.S. News’s requests for information.

But those surveys, opinions and strategies have not stopped many schools, eager for any edge that could entice students in a stormy era for higher education, from marketing their place in the rankings. U.S. News has acknowledged in the past that it sometimes ranked more schools because more of them “wanted to be paid attention to.”

This year, U.S. News rolled out rankings for undergraduate economics programs and in-state schools it thought offered the best value.

The publisher attributed the overall increase in the number of ranked schools to changes to the Carnegie Classification, a system that categorizes schools on the basis of, say, research activity.

item.title: Grand Jury Finds Insufficient Evidence of Crime in Death of Nolan Wells
item.description:
A grand jury in Mississippi has concluded that there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges in the case of Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old who was found dead two days after a boat outing with friends on July 4.

The grand jury in Jackson County, Miss., found unanimously that the circumstances and condition of Mr. Wells’s body were “consistent with drowning,” according to a copy of its report posted on social media on Monday by the county district attorney’s office. It also said there was no credible evidence of criminal conduct by the people who traveled with him to an island off the Mississippi coast that day.

The report noted that both the state’s chief medical examiner and the forensic pathologist hired by the Wells family said the cause and manner of death were undetermined, and that drowning was a “diagnosis of exclusion.” The grand jury said that while there was bruising on the back of Mr. Wells’s neck, it was not a fatal injury, and its cause was uncertain.

The disappearance and death of Mr. Wells, who was Black, drew national attention. Civil rights activists, elected officials and social media users speculated about the circumstances of the case and the actions of the friends with whom he went to the island.

Mississippi’s history of racial injustice and the failure at times of its authorities to thoroughly look into crimes against Black people were factors in the conversations.

The grand jury report, submitted to a county circuit clerk on Friday, found that Mr. Wells was not the only Black person on the island that day. The report refuted what it said were “false assertions that have led to misidentification, speculation, and rumors” about his death.

“There is absolutely no evidence to support the allegations that Nolan’s disappearance and death were racially motivated,” Angel Myers McIlrath, the Jackson County district attorney, said on Monday in a video posted on social media along with the grand jury report.

The 23 people on the grand jury included five Black members, according to their report.

Ben Crump, the civil rights lawyer representing the Wells family, said in a statement on Monday that the grand jury’s report failed to determine what caused the injury on the back of Mr. Wells’s head and how it may have contributed to his death.

“Today, the state of Mississippi is attempting to close the chapter on Nolan Wells’s death without getting to the truth,” Mr. Crump said.

“We don’t know how Nolan died, and neither does the State of Mississippi,” he added, urging the authorities to continue their investigations.

Mr. Wells graduated from Ocean Springs High School in 2025 and played wide receiver last season for the Southwest Mississippi Community College football team. He was last seen alive on July 4, when he went by boat with friends to Horn Island, an unpopulated, 10-mile-long strip.

His friends returned to the mainland without him, with one later saying that Mr. Wells had stayed behind because he had met a girl on the island. When he did not return later that night, his mother reported him missing. Multiple agencies began a search, and a park ranger found his body on July 6.

The grand jury’s report said Mr. Wells and his friends traveled on three boats to Horn Island, and that he and some others chose to remain there to socialize after the boats departed. The names of the people who went to the island with Mr. Wells were redacted in the report released by the district attorney’s office.

One of the questions raised earlier in the case concerned Mr. Wells’s belongings, including his phone, which his friends brought back to the mainland. The grand jury found that it was not unusual for people to return from the island on different boats than they had taken to get there or for their personal items to be sent back without them. Its report said that Mr. Wells’s was not the only phone to return without its owner to the mainland that day.

The report noted, however, that there is no statute of limitations in Mississippi for homicide cases, and that if any evidence emerges suggesting that the death of Mr. Wells was not accidental, it should be referred to the grand jury for consideration.
